8	
9	A fact is a finding that is an established property of the tree, the language, the library or their tools, and that later work builds on. A defect also gets its ledger row, and a fact about it may cite the row.
10	
11	A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.
12	
13	Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:
14	
15	- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
16	- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
17	- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
18	- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
19	- **For FACTS.** Each fact that your work established, in the hand-over form of "Writing to the record". If your brief let you write FACTS, give instead the number of each entry that you added or rewrote. If your work established no fact, write "none".
20	- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
21	- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.
22	
23	## At a point to report
24	
25	- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
26	- Then finish the work.
27	- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
28	
29	## Timings and citations
30	
31	- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
32	- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
33	- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
34	- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.
35	
36	## POSITIONS and FACTS
37	
38	POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them. When your work needs the detail of an entry, print the report section that it cites (`$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'`, below). Read its history only when the tree disagrees with the entry.
39	
40	Each entry is one line that starts with its permanent number: `F-87` in FACTS, `P-48` in POSITIONS. A FACTS entry is the fact as it stands now, what it means for the work, and the test that fails if the fact stops holding, under a bold title. If no test checks the fact, the entry gives the command and the output that show it. It points to the report section that holds the detail. Cite an entry by its number. If the reader must know what the entry says without printing it, add the first words of its title in quotes: F-87, "The first words ...".
41	
42	## The gap ledger
43	
44	The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).
45	
46	A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.
47	
48	- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
49	- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
50	- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.
51	
52	Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.
53	
54	A row states its gap as it stands now. A note adds a fact. If your work changes what a row says, write the row's whole new line with `rewrite` (below), not a note that tells the repair.
55	
56	The heading reader of `ledger.py` does not expand the specification's `\Trait{X}` macro. So a row that names a library trait's section cites `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by line.
57	
58	## Reading the record
59	
60	Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:
61	
62	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
63	
64	- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
65	- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
66	- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
67	- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
68	- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
69	- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
70	- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
71	- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.
72	
73	A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.
74	
75	Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:
76	
77	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE
78	
79	## Writing to the record
80	
81	- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
82	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
83	- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
84	  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
85	  - what it means for the work;
86	  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
87	  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
88	  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
89	- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
90	- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
91	- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.
92	
93	Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.
94	
95	    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"
96	
97	To add a row:
98	
99	1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
100	2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
101	3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.
102	
103	To change a row:
104	
105	- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N. It refuses a note that takes the row past 1,200 characters, or its notes cell past 700 characters. `$L note N TEXT --check` writes nothing. It says whether TEXT fits, and how many characters the notes and the row have left now and would have left with TEXT. These counts include the separator that the tool adds. It exits 0 if TEXT fits, and 1 if not. Run it before a long note, or before a note on a row near its limits. If TEXT does not fit, shorten it, or cut the notes with `rewrite` (below).
106	- `$L rewrite N FILE` replaces row N with the whole line in FILE, a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with N or `?` in its number cell. Use it to correct the claim, cut the notes or change the reproducer. The tool checks the line against the template and keeps the old line in the history file.
107	- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
108	- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it. NAME can also be a file under `explorations/coordinator/tools/`, or `none` with `--note REASON`. For a `CONTESTED` row, add `--settled TEXT`, which names what settled its question.
109	- `$L landing-check BASE` prints each problem, and exits 1 on any. Run it when your brief asks for it. It checks the whole ledger against the template, so a broken row that BASE already had counts too. The problems are a row that breaks the template, an `XXX` test deleted or renamed while a row that is not closed names it, a row that is not closed though a commit says it fixed it, and a FACTS or POSITIONS entry that disagrees with a row's status.
110	
111	## The repository's history
112	
113	- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
114	- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
115	- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
116	- If the commands above fail, run `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`. It prints `true` in a shallow clone, where these commits do not resolve. There, a copyright header of Sun Microsystems or Oracle, as in `Library/Format.fss`, marks a file that the team made, but not which of its lines the port or the revival changed. If your task needs those lines, say in your report that the clone is shallow.
117	- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
118	- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.
119	- Commit `8fe1daa8f` copied a third-party port of the tree to Java 9 onto the team's last commit, `a874948ac`. Give its lines no credit, and name no author of it in any text that you commit. In a reconstruction of authorship, attribute nothing of it to anyone.

- F-93 **A generator's size is a counted default on `Generator`, the relational predicate reads neither a size nor an index, and `Indexed`'s default index-value pairs keep the indexed value's indices.** A type with its own `|self|` keeps it. Two answers differ from the team's library: `increasing((0#4).reverse)` fails where it held, and the default pairs of a value indexed from 5 are indexed from 5, not 0. Gated by `tests/GeneratorSize.fss`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generator-size/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6.
- F-94 **The compiled checker checks the array family under the bound `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`, and calls through a parameter so bounded.** Its refusals and crashes there (rows 686, 687, 689, 690), the library's `squaredNorm(me)` among them, had one cause, the normal form's expansion of the closed trait over a conjunct that names the variable, which F-227 gives. A memo on the trait table keeps the count stage within its 900-second limit (row 688). Gated by `OverloadTwoBoundsClosed*` and `compiler_tests/*TwoBoundsClosedTrait`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-array-bound/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 9; `compile-ladder/rung-checker-bounds/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-220 **`__bigOperator`'s local function `body` declares its parameter's type, `body(i: I): L` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss`), and the compiled checker accepts the line.** The distance stage and the checker count find no error at the line (F-53). F-228 holds how walk runs it: a reduction or a comprehension that writes no static argument is instantiated by its value's declared type, else its elements' join, else its bound. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-elements/REPORT.md` section 6.
- F-221 **The compiled checker retries a call written as another call's argument against each enclosing declaration's parameter type, where the enclosing call is not accepted otherwise.** It builds P-51 under P-49, so a declaration that accepts the call as written is never passed over. A reduction's plain-bounded big operator, an argument of `__bigOperator` once desugared, so takes the reduction's expected type; one whose bound names its parameter takes that type, else its body's (F-364). A chain `a OPLUS b OPLUS c` that only the retry makes acceptable to a multifix declaration now runs it, not the binary one. Walk gives such an argument no expected type (row 705). Gated by `compiler_tests/InferCallArgument*` and `InferBigOperatorExpectedType`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-argument-context/REPORT.md` sections 1, 5 and 8, and `SKEPTIC.md` finding 5.
- F-225 **In a self-typed trait with no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as `C[\X\] & X`, the trait met with the implementing type, read from the trait's F-bound; the methods' signatures keep `self` at the plain trait type `C[\X\]`, save in the overloading check's exclusion test (F-277) and in the Return Type check of a dotted method redeclared below the trait (row 1094), and the checker refuses an extender at another type.** It builds P-146. A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`. The Return Type check reads `self` as `C[\X\] & X` in the trait's signature where an object's dotted method redeclares the trait's method at the same parameter types, so it refuses a narrower return type; a getter so redeclared reads the plain type and compiles (F-394). That reading of a dotted method departs from P-146 and P-157, which keep the plain signatures for the Return Type Rule (row 1094). The checker also takes a parameter bounded by a self-typed trait that the trait extends at that parameter, as the team's `Containment` mixins are: a default of the coordinator's. In a trait whose `comprises` clause lists types, `self` in the bodies is instead the trait met with the union of those types, and, as in a self-typed trait, the signatures keep `self` at the plain trait type and the exclusion test reads the meet. P-146 names the self-typed traits only; this reading of a `comprises` trait is a default of a batch's plan, which the curator has not decided. For example, `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, since `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. The rule accepts every self-typed body of the library but `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead (P-146). Walk has no such rule and loads what it refuses. A compiled default body that returns `self` at the self-type parameter runs, also where the parameter is an object type, as in `object Pt(…) extends Shape[\Pt\]` (row 695, fixed). F-377 gives the cast that does it, also at a conditional's arm and at a closure's result (rows 1051 and 1050, fixed). A default body that calls a method on a value of the self-type parameter runs, also where the object lists the trait first (row 1052, fixed); F-385 gives how, and the generic object for which it may not hold. The rule refuses, rightly, a team declaration, `PureList`'s `List` (row 355). The compiler's prelude writes the self type instead as `comprises T` on `StandardTotalOrder` and `Equality` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi`), and that spelling does not bind the one library, since Naden's last text puts the self-type idiom in bounds only, not as a first-class type (`Papers/Types/journal/justificationOfRTR.tex:626-630`), and Steele's own message on `655e65d53` gives the self type as the trait met with the `comprises` clause, which this rule reads from the F-bound. Gated by `compiler_tests/SelfType*` and `XXXSelfType*`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-self-type/REPORT.md` sections 1, 2, 4 and 7; `compile-ladder/rung-self-type-exclusion/REPORT.md` section 1.
- F-226 **The compiled checker renames an inherited method's own static parameters apart before it uses them: from the static parameters of the trait or object that inherits it, in the overloading check, and from the receiver's static arguments at a call.** So `Generator.generate[\R\]`, inherited by `PossibleReductionPair[\R\]`, keeps its own `R` (row 561). At a call, `commonInheritedMethods` (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala`) instantiates each method that the receiver's type inherits at the static arguments of its declaring trait. It first renames each of the method's own static parameters whose name those arguments mention to `name$i`, with `i` the least positive integer that gives an unused name; the checker's messages print that form (row 627). The same function builds the methods that a trait's body sees, so a call of an inherited method by its bare name inside a trait gets the same renaming. Gated by `compiler_tests/InheritedMethodStaticParamSameName`, `InheritedMethodByNameStaticParamSameName` and `MethodStaticArgReceiverSameName`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-overloading-checker/REPORT.md` section 6 (the overloading check); `compile-ladder/rung-checker-expected-type/REPORT.md` section 1 (the call).
- F-227 **The compiled checker replaces a closed trait among an intersection's conjuncts by those of its listed types that no other conjunct excludes, only where that excluding conjunct names no type variable or inference variable, so `K ∩ R[\T\]` stays as written; below a union, an inference variable takes the whole union as one upper bound, and a type variable is tried through its bound as well as against each member.** The code is `normConjunct` and, for the union cases, `pSubInner`, in `scala_src/types/TypeAnalyzer.scala`. So a call through a parameter bounded by a closed trait and a bound that excludes one of its listed types checks, and a generic declaration so bounded, beside a declaration on the closed trait, is a valid overloading (rows 686, 687, 689, 690 and 711). A call whose argument's type only carries the parameter, `Box[\T\]`, under a ground second bound, stays refused: an open defect (row 712). Before the checker kept such an intersection as written, it accepted, through the expansion, an overloading on a question that Appendix I lists as not settled; it refused the pair while it kept the intersection, and accepts it again since its exclusion test reads the static parameters' bounds (F-277; `compiler_tests/OverloadTwoBoundsClosedTraitExclusion`); walk refuses it at load (row 713, contested; `tests/OverloadTwoBoundsClosedTraitExclusionWalk`). Gated by `compiler_tests/*TwoBoundsClosedTrait` and `*TwoGroundBounds*ClosedTrait`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-bounds/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6.
- F-231 **The generated AST walker is split into eight methods that the JVM compiles; as one method it ran interpreted and took most of the checker's time.** `Walker.walk`, which `ScalaAstGenerator` writes into `FortressAst.scala`, was one method of 31,704 bytes, past HotSpot's 8,000-byte limit for compiling a method, and the checker's substitutions and normalizations all go through it. The split, in order and with identical output, was measured on climb batch 15's code with the repair that lets the checker check a block's local functions (row 680; F-233), the two changes that climb batch 15b then landed, on an idle machine. It took the count stage from 911 s to about 340 s and the distance stage from 2,375 s to 931 s; every run had the repair. In the library component's type check, about 95 % of the time that remained was the solver reducing formulas again, which its memos now answer (F-235). F-240 gives the stages' times now. Gated by `WalkerJUTest`, which fails if a method of `Walker` passes 8,000 bytes and checks the split walker's answers. Detail: `perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md` sections 2 and 6.
- F-232 **The syntax tree's hashes do not depend on the JVM's identity hashes, except at inference variables, walk's wrapped values and the nodes that hold them.** Every generated node's hash starts from the hash of its class's name: makeAST's post-processing of ASTGen's output writes that start, and so do the in-repo generators (`build.xml:698-716`). A field whose type holds an `Option` is hashed by `NodeHash.of` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes_util/NodeHash.java`), since the PLT `Option` classes hash by identity. So hash maps and sets of nodes that hold neither exception iterate in one order whatever code asked for an identity hash before, and so do the apis that `StaticChecker.checkApis` takes in turn. The exceptions hash through identity hashes: an inference variable's id is a bare `Object` (`nodes_util/NodeFactory.java:1166-1184`), but no output of the count stage moves through its hash; walk's `_WrappedFValue` hashes its `FValue` by walk's own hash, which can be an identity hash (`interpreter/evaluator/_WrappedFValue.java:170-177`; row 430). `DeclaredFunction`s, entries of the checker's index and not nodes, still hash by identity, but since row 737's repair no choice of `ApiTypeExtractor` depends on their order (F-254), and no choice among a call's declarations does (F-408). Gated by `NodeHashJUTest`, and row 737's repair by `OmittedReturnTypeFromApi`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-ast-hashes/REPORT.md` sections 4.2 to 4.4.
- F-233 **The compiled checker types a block's local functions with their group in scope.** So a local function with no written return type whose body calls another member of its group, as `Array3`'s `asString` does, checks; one that calls itself is refused for its reference cycle, as a top-level function is. Gated by `compiler_tests/LocalFunctionSiblingInLoop`, `LocalFunctionSiblingCall` and `XXXLocalFunctionRecursiveUntypedReturn`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-bounds/REPORT.md` section 6.
- F-235 **The compiled checker reduces a formula once in each analyzer, answers an exclusion asked again with fresh inference variables from a memo, and finds a type by its name once per trait table.** Each memo's key holds every input its answer reads: the formula, on the analyzer (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:601-621`); the exclusion question with its inference variables renamed apart, from an empty cycle history, shared through the trait table where it read no context (`:412-443`, `:994-1024`; `TraitTable.scala:150-156`); the name (`TraitTable.scala:34-68`). An answer that read the context is marked, one that opened a size is not kept, and each memo has a switch, default on (`fortress.analyzer.reduce.cache`, `fortress.analyzer.exclusion.cache`, `fortress.analyzer.typecons.cache`). The count stage went from 437 s to 97 s in one session, its tables and whole outputs equal, and audits that computed every reused answer again found 0 differences. A new memo of the checker follows the same rule. Gated by `ReductionMemoJUTest`, `ExclusionMemoJUTest` and `TraitTableMemoJUTest`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-solver-speed/REPORT.md` sections 1, 4, 6 and 7.
- F-236 **Every method of the build is within HotSpot's 8,000-byte limit but twelve, and a misc-track test fails when that changes.** `MethodSizeJUTest` reads every class of `ProjectFortress/build` with `java.lang.classfile`; it fails on an unlisted method past the limit and on a listed one gone from the build or back under it, and each entry of its list carries its size and what runs it. The twelve: `NodeReader.readNode`, the three parsers' `pCharLiteralContent$1`, `ExprDisambiguator.walk`, `Misc.checkExprMisc`, `HygienicRenamer.walk` (nothing constructs a `HygienicRenamer`), `MagicNumbers.<clinit>` and four `DirectedRoundingTestData` data methods that no suite runs. `WalkerJUTest` still guards `Walker` (F-231). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-solver-speed/REPORT.md` section 8.
- F-237 **The well-formedness walk reports an ill-formed type whose span lies outside the expression that the walk is in at that expression, so a call whose static argument breaks the bound of the callee's result type is reported at the call.** A call's type keeps the spans of the callee's declared type. An error on such a type is reported at the innermost expression the walk met it in, once for each call that made the type: the expressions that a call's value flows to share its type node and add no error, and a second call with the same printed static argument gets its own error. One known gap, still open (row 776): of two nested calls of one callee at static arguments that print alike, `next[\T\](next[\T\](x))`, only the inner call is reported; the program is still refused. Where the type is ill-formed where it is written, its error stays at the declaration. A local variable's right-hand side is walked before the lines that use the variable, so a call whose value a variable holds is reported at the call, not at a later use. In the library, by reading, reporting at the call adds and drops no error against reporting at the declaration, and the distance holds no well-formedness error (F-53). Source: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TypeWellFormedChecker.scala`, `check`, `error`, `outside` and `within`, and its `SLocalVarDecl` case. Gated by `compiler_tests/XXXStaticArgBoundAtCall`, `XXXStaticArgBoundAtCallOnce`, `XXXStaticArgBoundAtEachCall`, `XXXStaticArgBoundAtCallNotAtUse` and `XXXIllFormedTypeAtDeclarationOnce`, and `XXXStaticArgBoundNestedCall`, which pins row 776's single error. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-abstract-callsite/REPORT.md` sections 1 and 6, its `SKEPTIC.md` sections 5.1 and 5.2 and its `JUDGE.md`.
- F-240 **The checker's count stage takes about 65 s and its distance stage 117 s at the last landed gate, climb batch 36's.** At climb batch 15b's gate they took 325 s and 1,075 s; the solver's memos (F-235) make most of the difference, not load. Its rise from about 90 s at climb batch 21b's gate is the `FortressLibrary` component's check now run to its end, past its cleared type errors into the export check, not load: rung runs that stopped at those errors took 91 s and 99 s, runs past them 149 s and 151 s, one run each. Since climb batch 21b the checker checks every symbolic operator (F-281), which costs the count stage about 15 to 25 % by its rung's timings of its base and its head in one session. From climb batch 22's gate to climb batch 26's it stayed between about 150 s and 180 s. The count table records no seconds, so its time is the file times of the gate's log; the distance stage (`FortressLibrary` 75 s), over fourteen components, ran at a start load of 0.29, then beside the first minutes of `testFast`, so its time is one under that suite's load, against 130 s (85 s) at 0.55 at climb batch 35b's. Both stages about halved at climb batch 27's gate, and no run measured why: each gate ran each stage once, and neither the emptied `Number` (F-324) nor the distance's check stopped at `Char` (F-54) is shown to be the cause. Load can lengthen a stage more than twofold: climb batch 16's merged code took 217 s for the distance stage at its gate, at a load average of 3.3, and nearly the same code took 574 s at 4.6 to 5.3. So a time compares only with one taken under a like load. Source: the file times of the gate's log and `compile-ladder/climb-batch-36/gate/distance.txt`. Detail: `reviews/batch-31-review.md`, section 4; `reviews/batch-32-review.md`, section 4; `reviews/batch-27-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-26-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-25-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-24-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-23-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-22c-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-22-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-21b-review.md`, section 2; `reviews/batch-17-review.md`, section 1; `reviews/batch-16-review.md`, section 2.
- F-242 **`SUM`'s fusion pairs with `MAX` and `MIN` hold no site of the distance: a `where` condition on each of `SumReduction`'s two `distribute` overloads clears their four unmet bounds, and `ActualReduction`'s generic `distribute`, which `SumReduction` inherits, with its result over its own `K`, clears their two return-type errors.** The fusion pairs are `MaxSumReductionPair`, `MinSumReductionPair` and those two overloads, through which the team's `Generator2` computes the maximum or the minimum of sums in one pass. The two errors were at the two overloads, which answer a pair over `Maybe[\T\]` beside the inherited `distribute`. With the inherited one answering `PossibleReductionPair[\K\]`, they pass the return-type rule (F-75). The team's commented text, which answers `PossibleReductionPair[\R\]`, only moves the two errors to the generic. The fusion stays (P-151). Row 433, fixed; F-250 gives the landing and its test. Detail: `perf-probes/where-clauses/REPORT.md` A.1 and A.2.1; `perf-probes/generic-distribute/REPORT.md` sections 3 and 4.

- F-243 **The 13 errors that were filed as waiting on `where` clauses, 13 of the distance's 49 at the gates of climb batches 15b and 16, are all cleared; the 13th, the list comparisons' site, by conditional extension.** The where-clauses probe traced each of them (A.1). The method condition and the generic `distribute` clear the fusion pairs' 6 (F-242). `AnyList`'s `comprises { List[\E\] } where [\E\]` clause, a comment of the team's made live, clears its 4, with its bodies respelled within `AnyList` and none moved into `List` (F-251). A `cast` at `additiveIdentity`'s and `multiplicativeIdentity`'s fallbacks, `else => 0` and `else => 1`, clears 2 (row 436). Conditional extension cleared the list comparisons' site (the list half of row 634; its tuple half was built earlier), with `ZeroIndexed[\E\]` and an element-wise `=` kept outside the condition (F-255). By the probe, library edits with no new language would also have cleared 12: dropping the fusion pairs, moving `AnyList`'s bodies into `List`, and the `cast` at the fallbacks. Detail: `perf-probes/where-clauses/REPORT.md` A.0, A.1, A.4, B.0 and B.3; `reviews/batch-17-review.md`, section 2.
- F-244 **The three `where` forms that the checker builds (P-151: conditional extension, a function's or a method's condition, and `AnyList`'s `comprises` clause) hold where the where-clauses probe tested them; of the probe's two holes, one stands: a member checked under a conditional extension's condition stays callable where the condition fails (row 773; F-255).** A type variable opened from a `comprises` clause passes the probe's escape, two-value and Amin–Tate tests: the opened type is refused where another type is declared, two values get two types, and Amin and Tate's unsound shape is refused (F-251). The other hole is closed: a method's constraint on its trait's parameter bounds that parameter inside the method and is checked at a dotted call (row 748; F-256). Swift, Rust and Haskell scope such a member to the condition (B.3), which P-151 holds as still to build. The opening of a `comprises` clause has two other open rows of the gap ledger in the checker, 751 and 752; a third, row 775, a crash on such a trait's override, is fixed (F-281). F-250 (row 470) and F-256 give the constraints that the checker does not yet read. Detail: `perf-probes/where-clauses/REPORT.md` B.1 to B.3 and B.6.
- F-245 **With every symbolic operator checked for overloading, the compiled checker finds 5 errors in the library on climb batch 21's first run's code, the distance's 5, where that batch's base gave 191.** The checker checks every operator (F-281), so the distance stage is this check; it gave these 5 with no crash, and gives 0 since climb batch 22 cleared them (F-53). The 191 were measured by the full-check stage, a copy of the checker with every operator admitted that caught crashes per name (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/run-shadow.sh`), whose edits no longer match the tree; on climb batch 21's first run's code it caught the `AnyList` crash on `||` (row 809, fixed). Of the base's 186 errors beyond the 5, the library's known fixes clear 54 (F-276), the index bound 124 (F-278, P-156) and the exclusion test 8 (F-277, P-157); measured together on the merged tree, nothing comes. Walk's meet check skips symbolic operators (row 611); widened the same way at `d212b2c1f`, it refused only `EmptyString`'s `||` (F-142). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-symbolic-check/REPORT.md` section 5; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-21/RECORD.md`, "The tests on the merged tree"; `reviews/batch-21-review.md`, section 1; `perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md` sections 0 to 2; `perf-probes/symbolic-operators/REPORT.md` section 1.5.

So the checker gives an argument whose trait lists `Box[\E\] where [\E\]` a fresh type for the call, bounded by the bound of the clause's binding, `[\E extends B\]`, and by the clause's constraints on it (F-256). It refuses that type in a place whose declared type is another type, and it gives two values two types. It also refuses the shape of Amin and Tate's 2016 unsoundness example, where such a value would prove a subtype relation that does not hold. It does not open such a trait where it reaches it as a parent (row 752). Walk binds the variable as a symbolic type at load. On the rung's own tree the distance went from 49 to 45, row 636's four sites: `AnyList`'s `||` is now accepted through the opened type, and its `addLeft`, `addRight` and the list comprehension's unwrap were respelled. It takes the return type only if exactly one api declaration of the name matches. With none or several, it takes none, and the declaration is left as written. A clause that binds a variable, or that holds a constraint that is not a trait constraint, is read as before: as a parent at every instance.
